Less variable joint motions produce a less variable release point and therefore more accurate pitches.

Indirect: higher-level pitchers show less variability in many variables ([Fleisig et al., 2009](R-fleisig-2009-variability)). Motor-control theory predicts that joint variability that is compensated at the hand does not affect release ([Todorov and Jordan, 2002](R-todorov-2002-optimal)).
How much joint variability is compensated (structure, not size); how much is measurement error; whether release-point variability limits this pitcher's command at all.
Has changing the variable improved performance?
No intervention study shows that reducing joint-angle variability improves command.
Does the improvement transfer to competition?
Unknown; transfer to game command would require competitive outcome measures.
What are the implications for loading or potential injury-related risk?
Unknown; constraining movement variability might concentrate repetitive loading on the same tissue regions, a hypothesis rather than a finding.

apply.text: Applying the ideas to pitching and hitting

For a pitcher, the useful questions are which task variables matter (release location, release direction, velocity, spin axis), how variable each is, and whether joint-level variability is compensated. A pitcher whose trunk tilt varies but whose arm angle relative to the trunk co-varies to keep release height stable is showing coordination, not inconsistency. A pitcher whose release height wanders with his trunk tilt may have a command problem with a mechanical source worth investigating.

For a hitter, the task variables are bat-path timing and bat orientation at contact relative to a pitch that varies. Here variability is partly the point: a hitter must produce different swings for different pitches. Swing-to-swing variability against a tee says little about adaptability against live pitching, and reducing it in tee work is not obviously desirable.

A worked estimate shows why structure matters. Treat the arm from shoulder to hand as a 0.6 m lever. A 2° error in its orientation (0.035 rad) moves the hand by about 0.6 × 0.035 ≈ 2.1 cm. If variations in trunk tilt and in shoulder angle each move the hand by about 2 cm in the same direction and are independent, their effects add in quadrature to about 3 cm; if they are negatively correlated, so that a larger tilt comes with a smaller shoulder angle, the hand moves much less than either variation alone would predict. Release-point variability therefore cannot be read off joint-angle variability without knowing the correlations among joints — the core idea of the uncontrolled manifold.

Newell's framework gives a structured way to generate hypotheses. For a pitcher whose stride is shorter than his peers', list candidate organismic constraints (hip mobility, lead-leg strength), environmental constraints (mound slope, footing) and task constraints (pitch type, intent, the drill), then decide which measurements would distinguish them before prescribing a change.

apply.title: Executive twist: a 'consistency score' in a development dashboard

blocks.text: A proposed dashboard ranks pitchers by a single 'mechanical consistency score' averaged over twenty joint angles. Motor-control theory and the measurement literature both argue against it: it mixes task-relevant and task-irrelevant variability, includes measurement error, and implies that less variability is always better. A defensible alternative reports variability of task outcomes (release point, velocity, location) with measurement error stated, and analyses joint variability only to explain outcome variability that matters.

retain.text: Redundancy means many movements achieve one goal. Variability that leaves the goal unchanged is not error, and optimal-feedback control predicts that skilled performers will allow it. Constraints of body, environment and task shape which solution an athlete uses. The questions for any variability measure are: in which dimension, how much is measurement error, and does it matter for the outcome?
What does the uncontrolled-manifold method partition, and what does a high ratio of along-manifold to across-manifold variance indicate?
Give one organismic, one environmental and one task constraint that could change a hitter's swing.
Why is a single average 'consistency score' over many joints hard to interpret?

takeaways: The body is redundant: many joint combinations produce the same task outcome.
Variability in task-irrelevant dimensions is expected and can be functional; variability that changes the outcome is the concern.
Optimal feedback control predicts minimal intervention: correct only deviations that threaten the goal.
Organismic, environmental and task constraints together shape individual movement solutions.
Measured variability includes measurement error, which must be estimated before variability is interpreted.

check.explanation: Variance along the manifold leaves hand position unchanged; variance across it changes hand position. Much more variance along than across indicates that the joints compensate for one another to stabilize the hypothesized task variable.

optionFeedback.c: Measurement error would not produce this specific structure; it is a separate question.
optionFeedback.d: The structure is evidence that hand position is stabilized.

exercise.title: The Biomechanics Foundations Lab

intro.text: This laboratory has four stations. Each is mathematically exact where it computes geometry or mechanics, and explicitly illustrative where it models coordination. Work through them in order; each takes about ten minutes, and each ends with a question to answer in your own words before you move on.

items: **Station 1 — Rotation sequences.** Set a segment's orientation with one Cardan sequence and three sliders. The lab re-describes the identical orientation under every other sequence, including the ISB Y–X–Y humeral sequence. Reproduce the Lesson 2 flagship orientation by setting X–Z–Y to (−67°, 28°, 71°) and compare the axial rotation reported under Z–X–Y and Y–X–Y; note that the lab shows the Y–X–Y branch with positive elevation. Then push a middle angle toward ±89° and watch the first and third angles of other sequences jump: gimbal lock.

**Station 2 — Reference frames.** Tilt the trunk toward the glove side while keeping the arm's abduction relative to the trunk fixed. The lab reports the arm relative to the trunk and relative to the laboratory vertical. Find a trunk tilt that makes a 90° shoulder abduction look like a high arm slot in the laboratory frame.

**Station 3 — Force and moment.** Set a force, its distance from an axis and the angle between the lever and the force. The lab computes the moment τ = r·F·sin θ, draws the moment arm and states the direction by the right-hand rule. Confirm the Lesson 3 example (200 N at 0.30 m, perpendicular: 60 N·m) and find a different force and angle that give the same moment.

**Station 4 — Kinetic-chain timing (illustrative).** Adjust the gap between peak pelvis, trunk, elbow-extension and shoulder internal-rotation angular velocities in a teaching model with bell-shaped curves, and compare two preset athletes. The model is not physiological and computes no ball or bat speed. It exists to make sequencing and timing concrete and to make you state what a real study would have to measure.

intro.text: Before Station 1, predict how different the three reported axial rotations will be for the flagship orientation. Before Station 4, predict what changing the timing gap will do to modelled ball speed — and then check what the model actually contains.

tasks.prompt: Set the orientation with **X–Z–Y = (−67°, 28°, 71°)**, the Lesson 2 flagship. Before reading the table, predict the **third (axial-rotation) angle** the same orientation receives under **Z–X–Y**.
tasks.explain: The engine extracts all sequences from one rotation matrix. Axial rotation is about 119° under Z–X–Y against 71° under X–Z–Y: a definitional difference of nearly 50° for an unchanged arm.

tasks.prompt: Same orientation. Predict the **elevation** (second angle) reported under the ISB **Y–X–Y** sequence. Hint: elevation is the angle between the humerus and the thorax's long axis, which does not depend on how the other two angles are split.
tasks.explain: Elevation is about 70° whatever the sequence used to set the orientation, because it is a single angle between two axes. The plane of elevation and axial rotation, by contrast, depend on the branch the software reports (here about −150° and −120°, equivalent to 30° and 60° with negative elevation).

tasks.prompt: Set Z–X–Y with its **middle angle at 89°** and move the first slider slowly. What happens to the angles reported under the other Cardan sequences that share the singular configuration?

options.text: Nothing; all sequences change smoothly by the same amount
First and third angles of a locked sequence change abruptly or trade off, because two axes nearly align (gimbal lock)
The segment itself jumps on the screen

tasks.explain: Near a middle angle of ±90° a Cardan sequence's first and third axes align, so only their sum or difference is well defined. The segment moves smoothly; only its description becomes unstable.

tasks.prompt: Trunk tilted **30°** toward the glove side, arm abducted **90°** relative to the trunk. Predict the arm's elevation relative to the **laboratory** downward vertical.
tasks.explain: In this frontal-plane model the laboratory elevation is abduction plus tilt: 120°, i.e. 30° above horizontal. The shoulder angle is ordinary; the high slot comes from the trunk.

tasks.prompt: Trunk tilt **20°**, arm abduction relative to the trunk **95°**. Predict the laboratory elevation.
tasks.explain: 95° + 20° = 115°, or 25° above horizontal. The same calculation appears in the Lesson 2 check question.

tasks.prompt: A **200 N** force acts **0.30 m** from the axis, perpendicular to the lever. Predict the moment.
tasks.explain: τ = r·F·sin θ = 0.30 × 200 × 1 = 60 N·m, the magnitude of the vector example in Lesson 3.

tasks.prompt: Now **400 N** at **0.30 m**, but at **30°** to the lever. Predict the moment.
tasks.explain: sin 30° = 0.5, so τ = 0.30 × 400 × 0.5 = 60 N·m. Doubling the force while halving the moment arm (0.15 m) gives the same moment.

tasks.prompt: In this illustrative model, what happens to **ball speed** when you lengthen the gap between peaks from 20 ms to 60 ms?

options.text: It increases, because longer gaps transfer more energy
It decreases, because the chain loses energy
Nothing; the model contains no ball speed, so it cannot say

tasks.explain: The station shows timing only. Any claim that a gap raises velocity would need data — ideally within athletes and from an intervention — not a teaching model.

tasks.prompt: Athlete A (40 ms gaps) throws harder than Athlete B (20 ms gaps). Which study would best test whether lengthening B's gaps would raise his velocity?

options.text: A larger cross-sectional comparison of pitchers with long and short gaps
A controlled intervention that changes timing, measuring velocity and arm kinetics before, after and at a retention test
Asking pitchers with long gaps how they feel

tasks.explain: Only an intervention tests whether changing the variable changes the outcome; measuring kinetics and retention addresses load and durability.

debrief.text: Stations 1 and 2 show the week's central measurement lesson: a joint angle is a description chosen by the analyst. One unchanged orientation produced angles that differ by tens of degrees, and a trunk tilt changed the arm's position in space without any change at the shoulder. Two reports disagree for these reasons more often than because one system is inaccurate. Station 3 is exact vector algebra; its practical value is the habit of checking which convention a report uses before reading a sign.

Station 4 does not show what a pitcher or hitter should do. Its curves are drawn from assumptions written into the model, not from data, and it ignores tissue loading, strength, the need to adjust a swing late, and individual anatomy. Real evidence on timing comes from studies such as those discussed in Lesson 4, almost all of them associations between athletes. The model deliberately contains no ball or bat speed, so no gap can be “better” inside it; any such ranking would have to come from data. Use it to ask what a study would need to measure — velocity, joint kinetics and timing, within athletes, before and after a change, with a retention test — not to set targets.

assumptions: Stations 1–3 use rigid-body mathematics: right-handed frames, intrinsic rotations about mobile axes (R = R1·R2·R3), angles in degrees, forces in newtons and distances in metres; Station 3 reports the scalar moment r·F·sin θ in the plane of the figure.

Station 1's thorax frame has X anterior, Y superior and Z to the right; the humeral Y axis points from the elbow toward the shoulder. Sign conventions are shown on screen and can differ from those of a given laboratory.

Station 2 is a planar frontal-plane model that treats the trunk as one rigid segment, so laboratory elevation equals abduction plus tilt; in 3D, and in real trunks that bend and twist, the relationship is not a simple sum.

Station 4 is an explicitly illustrative teaching model of segment peak angular velocities (bell-shaped curves with fixed relative heights) with adjustable timing gaps. It is not a physiological or musculoskeletal model, contains no ball or bat speed, and makes no prediction about any athlete's velocity or injury risk.
No athlete data are used; all values are entered by the learner or are synthetic.

case.title: The Separation Claim
case.fiction: All people, organizations, studies and data in this case are fictional. The Mesa Verde Condors, Kestrel Valley University and its Throwing Performance Laboratory are invented for teaching; any resemblance to real organizations is coincidental.

body.text: Nadia Ferreira had been Director of Pitching Development for the Mesa Verde Condors for fourteen months when the press release arrived in her inbox with a subject line she knew the general manager would also be reading: “New study: hip–shoulder timing causes velocity.” The release came from the Throwing Performance Laboratory at Kestrel Valley University, a group with a growing reputation and a polished social-media presence. By lunchtime, two of the organization's minor-league pitching coaches had forwarded it to her with the same question: should they start the drill progression the laboratory was recommending for every pitcher in the system?

The study summary was two pages long. The laboratory had captured 48 college pitchers, each throwing eight fastballs, in a single session with a marker-based system and force plates. For each pitcher the researchers averaged the eight pitches and computed a variable they called pelvis–trunk delay: the time between peak pelvis angular velocity and peak upper-trunk angular velocity. Across the 48 pitchers, delay correlated positively with average ball velocity (r = 0.41). Pitchers in the top third for delay threw, on average, 1.9 m/s faster than pitchers in the bottom third. The summary concluded that “increasing pelvis–trunk delay is a primary driver of velocity” and that “training delay will add velocity.”

Nadia read the methods twice. The pitchers had been recruited from three nearby programs. Body mass and height were reported in a demographic table but did not appear in the analysis. The authors had tested 31 kinematic and kinetic variables for correlation with velocity and reported the five strongest; they did not mention a correction for multiple comparisons. There was no within-pitcher analysis, although each pitcher had thrown eight pitches. Elbow and shoulder kinetics had been computed, but the summary reported only that “arm kinetics were within normal ranges.” The drill progression recommended at the end of the summary had not been tested in the study.

She asked the organization's biomechanist, Theo Lindqvist, to look at it with her. Theo pointed out what the correlation could and could not support. An r of 0.41 meant that delay accounted for about 17% of the between-pitcher variance in velocity in this sample. The top-versus-bottom-third comparison exaggerated the difference by discarding the middle of the distribution. Larger, stronger pitchers might show both longer delays and higher velocity for reasons unrelated to timing itself; without body size or strength in the model, the association could be partly or largely a size effect. And because the variable was averaged within pitchers, the study said nothing about whether a given pitcher throws harder on the pitches where his delay is longer.

Theo also raised the kinetics. Studies in the published literature had found that timing variables can move ball speed and arm loads together. If a longer delay in this sample came with greater elbow varus moments, “within normal ranges” was not reassuring; it was simply unreported. He wanted the correlation between delay and normalized elbow moment before anyone changed a delivery.

The coaches had a different view. Marcus Bell, the pitching coordinator at the organization's high-A affiliate, had used a version of the drill progression for two seasons. “I've seen guys gain velocity,” he said in the meeting. “Not everybody, but enough. The study just confirms what we see.” Nadia asked how many pitchers had gained, how many had not, how velocity had been measured, and whether the pitchers had also changed their strength programs during that time. Marcus did not have those numbers. He did have conviction, and several pitchers who credited the drills.

Nadia understood the force of that experience and its limits. Young pitchers usually gain velocity over two seasons as they mature and train, with or without any one drill. Pitchers who improved were more likely to be remembered and to credit what they had been doing. And the drill itself changed several things at once — stride direction, intent, the timing cue — so even a real effect could not be attributed to delay.

The general manager's message arrived that afternoon. He wanted a recommendation by Friday: adopt the progression system-wide, pilot it, or ignore it. He added that a rival organization was rumoured to have hired someone from the Kestrel Valley laboratory, and that he did not want the Condors to be late to something real.

Nadia sketched three options. Adopting system-wide would be quick and would please the coaches who already believed in it, but it would make it impossible to tell whether the progression worked, and it would change the deliveries of pitchers who were throwing well. Ignoring the study would avoid a possible loading cost, but if delay was a real lever for some pitchers, the organization would lose time. A pilot would take a season, require pitchers to be assigned to the progression or to their usual program, demand consistent measurement of velocity, timing and arm kinetics before and after, and need a retention test weeks later to separate learning from a short-term change. It would also require coaches to accept that some of their pitchers would not receive the drill they believed in.

There was one more complication. The organization's motion-capture system defined the trunk segment differently from the laboratory's, and computed angular velocities from a different marker set. Theo was not sure that 'delay' measured on the Condors' system would match the laboratory's values; a bridging comparison would be needed before any number from the study could be used as a target.
Nadia opened a blank document and wrote the first line of her recommendation: “What the study observed, what it claims, and what we would need to know.” Then she began to fill in the seven questions.

questions: Apply the seven-question standard to the claim that “increasing pelvis–trunk delay is a primary driver of velocity.” Which of the five evidence categories (measurement, mechanical output, competitive outcome, intervention, retention and transfer) does the study address?
Name at least three alternative explanations for the between-pitcher correlation, and the analysis or data that would test each.
What would a defensible pilot look like? Specify assignment, measurements (including arm kinetics), timing of tests and the result that would stop the program.
How should Nadia handle the coaches' experience with the drills — as evidence, as a hypothesis, or as neither?
What has to happen before any delay value from the laboratory can be used with the Condors' capture system?

perspectives.title: Run a controlled pilot with load monitoring
perspectives.text: Treat delay as a hypothesis. Assign eligible pitchers to the progression or to usual training, matched on level and velocity, with equal total throwing volume. Measure velocity, delay and normalized arm kinetics on the same system before, after and six weeks later. Pre-specify what counts as success and what kinetic change would stop the progression. This is slower and frustrates believers, but it is the only option that produces an answer.

perspectives.title: Individualize instead of pilot
perspectives.text: Use the organization's own repeated-pitch data to estimate, for each pitcher, whether delay relates to velocity within him. Offer the progression only to pitchers whose within-pitcher data and physical profile suggest timing is a limiting factor, and track each one as a single-case design. This respects individual solutions but yields weaker group-level evidence.

perspectives.title: Decline for now and ask the laboratory for more
perspectives.text: Request the within-pitcher analysis, the kinetics and the size-adjusted results from the laboratory before committing resources. If the association survives adjustment for body mass and appears within pitchers, revisit. This avoids a possible loading cost and preserves coaching time, at the risk of moving late if the effect is real.

case.application: The case is about baseball, but its structure is general to any claim that a measured movement variable causes an outcome: a between-subject correlation, a mechanism that sounds right, an untested intervention, practitioner testimony and organizational pressure to act. In sports medicine, rehabilitation and ergonomics the same pattern appears whenever a posture or technique variable is linked to performance or injury. The response is the same in every field: classify the evidence, test alternative explanations, and evaluate the intervention itself with measurement that includes loading and retention.

questions.prompt: A lead-leg braking force rises linearly from 0 to 1,000 N over 0.04 s and falls linearly back to 0 over the next 0.08 s. Treat it as the net horizontal force on an 80 kg pitcher. By how much does his forward velocity decrease, in m/s?
questions.working: The force–time curve is a triangle with base 0.04 + 0.08 = 0.12 s and height 1,000 N. Impulse = ½ × 1,000 × 0.12 = 60 N·s. Δv = impulse / mass = 60 / 80 = 0.75 m/s.
questions.explanation: Impulse is the area under the force–time curve, and net impulse equals the change in linear momentum. The 60 N·s braking impulse slows the 80 kg pitcher by 0.75 m/s.

questions.prompt: Model the upper trunk as rotating about its longitudinal axis with moment of inertia 1.2 kg·m² (illustrative value). At a peak angular velocity of 1,100°/s, what is its angular momentum about that axis, in kg·m²/s?
questions.working: Convert to radians per second: 1,100 × π/180 ≈ 19.20 rad/s. L = I·ω = 1.2 × 19.20 ≈ 23.0 kg·m²/s.
questions.explanation: Angular momentum of a rigid segment about a principal axis is I·ω with ω in rad/s. Forgetting the degree-to-radian conversion inflates the answer by a factor of about 57.

questions.prompt: A bat rotates about an axis through the hands at 2,000°/s. Ignoring the hands' own motion, what is the speed of a point on the barrel 0.70 m from that axis, in m/s?
questions.explanation: Linear speed due to rotation is ω × r with ω in radians per second. The real barrel speed adds the hands' velocity vectorially, so this is the rotational contribution only.

questions.prompt: Two laboratories analyse the same pitch. Laboratory A reports 60° of humeral axial rotation using the ISB Y–X–Y sequence; Laboratory B reports 119° using a Z–X–Y sequence. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: One laboratory has a calibration error of about 60°.
The two values can describe the same orientation; they are not comparable without matching sequences and frames.
Laboratory B's value is more accurate because Cardan sequences avoid singularities.
The pitcher must have changed his arm action between the two analyses.

questions.explanation: Different sequences decompose the same rotation into different angles, and the axial-rotation angle is especially sensitive. In Lesson 2's flagship example, one orientation gives 60° under Y–X–Y and about 119° under Z–X–Y. The values are comparable only after matching definitions.

optionFeedback.a: A definitional difference of this size is expected; it does not imply measurement error.
optionFeedback.c: Cardan sequences also have singularities, at a middle angle of ±90°.
optionFeedback.d: It is the same pitch; no change in the arm is needed to produce different numbers.

questions.prompt: Read the fictional study summary. Which interpretation is best supported?

stimulus.text: Fictional study. Sixty high school hitters swung off a tee five times each. Average peak trunk angular velocity correlated with average bat speed across hitters (r = 0.52). Within hitters, swing-to-swing trunk angular velocity and bat speed correlated weakly (pooled within-hitter r = 0.08). The authors conclude that trunk rotation training will increase bat speed.

options.text: Trunk rotation training will increase bat speed, because the between-hitter correlation is moderate.
Hitters with faster trunks tend to have higher bat speed, but within a hitter trunk velocity and bat speed barely co-vary; neither result tests training.
The within-hitter correlation shows that trunk rotation does not affect bat speed in anyone.
The results generalize to game hitting because tee swings remove noise.

questions.explanation: The between-hitter correlation describes differences among hitters, which may reflect size, strength or skill. The weak within-hitter correlation means that swing-to-swing variation in trunk velocity barely relates to bat speed inside a hitter. Neither is an intervention, and tee conditions limit transfer to live pitching.

optionFeedback.a: A cross-sectional correlation does not demonstrate a training effect.
optionFeedback.c: Natural swing-to-swing variation is small and not an intervention; it cannot rule out an effect of a trained change.
optionFeedback.d: Tee swings remove the perceptual and timing demands of live pitching, which limits generalization.

questions.prompt: Identify the main flaw in the argument.

stimulus.text: Fictional argument. “His pelvis and trunk peak at almost the same time, so he has an energy leak. Energy that should have reached his arm is lost, which is why he throws 2 m/s slower than his teammate. Fix the sequence and he will gain that velocity back.”

options.text: It treats a kinematic timing description as proof of an energy loss and assumes that changing it will add a specific amount of velocity.
It uses metres per second instead of miles per hour.
It ignores that peak pelvis velocity should always come after peak trunk velocity.
It fails to mention that the teammate is taller.

questions.explanation: A kinematic sequence graph shows when segments peak, not where energy goes; energy flow has to be computed from kinetics. The argument also attributes a between-pitcher velocity difference to one variable and assumes an intervention effect of exactly that size.

optionFeedback.b: Units are not the flaw; m/s is the SI unit.
optionFeedback.c: Proximal-to-distal ordering puts the pelvis peak first, and the argument's timing claim is not the main error.
optionFeedback.d: Size could be a confound, but the central flaw is the unsupported leap from timing to energy loss to a guaranteed gain.

questions.prompt: Which response to the screen is most defensible?

stimulus.text: Hypothetical screen. A right-handed pitcher shows throwing-side passive internal rotation of 40° and external rotation of 110°; non-throwing side 62° and 103°. Measurements were taken by one clinician with a goniometer.

options.text: Prescribe daily stretching to restore internal rotation to the non-throwing value.
Compute the total arc (150° vs 165°), note the 15° total-arc deficit in addition to the expected shift, and refer for clinical evaluation, recognizing measurement error of several degrees.
Conclude that the pitcher will be injured this season.
Ignore it, because all throwers have less internal rotation.

questions.explanation: The throwing side's total arc is 150° against 165° on the other side, so beyond the expected shift toward external rotation there is a 15° total-arc deficit, a pattern associated with injury in one professional cohort. That justifies clinical evaluation, not a diagnosis or a prediction, and goniometric error must be kept in mind.

optionFeedback.a: Part of the internal-rotation difference is expected bony adaptation; the clinically relevant signal is the total-arc deficit, which needs evaluation rather than a generic prescription.
optionFeedback.c: Associations in cohorts are not individual predictions.
optionFeedback.d: The arc shift is expected, but the total-arc deficit is not.

questions.prompt: Which statements about movement variability are consistent with the motor-control ideas in this week? Select all that apply.

options.text: Skilled performers can vary joint angles from trial to trial while keeping a task variable stable.
Any reduction in joint-angle variability improves performance.
Optimal feedback control predicts that deviations are corrected mainly when they threaten the goal.
Measured variability includes measurement error that must be estimated before interpretation.
Elite pitchers reproduce identical deliveries on every pitch.

questions.explanation: Redundancy allows joint-level variability to be compensated so that a task variable stays stable; optimal feedback control predicts minimal intervention; and observed variability combines biological variability with measurement error. Neither elite invariance nor 'less variability is always better' is supported.

questions.prompt: Rank these designs from strongest to weakest evidence that changing pelvis–trunk timing increases a pitcher's velocity.

options.text: Cross-sectional correlation between timing and velocity across 50 pitchers
Randomized trial of a timing intervention versus usual training, with velocity measured after training and at a six-week retention test
Within-pitcher association between pitch-to-pitch timing variation and velocity
Testimonials from pitchers who used a timing drill

questions.explanation: Only a randomized intervention with retention directly tests whether changing timing raises velocity durably. A within-pitcher association at least addresses the right level of analysis, though natural variation is not an intervention. A between-pitcher correlation is open to confounding by size and strength. Testimonials are subject to recall and maturation biases.

questions.prompt: A vendor offers a dashboard that flags pitchers whose elbow varus moment exceeds the 80th percentile of its reference database. What is the best next move before adopting it?

options.text: Adopt it and shut down flagged pitchers immediately.

Ask how moments are computed and normalized relative to the reference population, whether velocity is accounted for, and use it for within-pitcher monitoring with clinical review rather than between-pitcher risk labels.
Reject it, because joint moments have no relationship to injury.
Adopt it but only for pitchers who throw above a velocity threshold.

questions.explanation: Net moments are model-dependent and rise with velocity, so between-pitcher percentiles mix size, velocity and method. The defensible use is consistent within-pitcher monitoring with clinicians involved, after the vendor's methods are understood.

optionFeedback.a: A single percentile flag is not an injury probability, and shutdown decisions belong to clinicians.
optionFeedback.c: Elbow valgus torque is among the few variables with some support as a risk factor; the issue is interpretation, not irrelevance.
optionFeedback.d: A velocity cut-off does not solve the comparability problem.

questions.prompt: Apply the seven-question standard to this claim from a training facility's website: “Our lead-leg bracing program increases bat speed because a stiffer front leg transfers more energy up the chain.” In 150–250 words, state what has been observed, the proposed mechanism, the evidence that would be needed, what remains uncertain, and any loading considerations.
questions.modelAnswer: Observed: likely between-hitter associations between lead-leg kinematics or ground reaction forces and bat speed, plus facility testimonials; no intervention data are cited. Mechanism: a braking lead leg slows forward motion and, with a ground reaction force passing in front of the centre of mass, generates angular momentum that trunk and arms redistribute; 'energy transfer' would need to be computed as energy flow, not inferred. Evidence needed: within-hitter associations, then a controlled intervention measuring bat speed (a mechanical output) before, after and at retention, ideally with live-pitch outcomes for transfer. Uncertain: whether bracing is a cause or a by-product of strength and skill; dose–response; effects on timing and adaptability against varied pitches; whether gains appear in games. Has changing the variable improved performance? Not shown by the claim. Transfer to competition? Unknown. Loading: greater braking forces load the lead knee and hip; this is not an injury probability, but volume and individual capacity should be monitored, with clinical input where relevant.

rubric.criterion: Separates evidence categories (measurement, mechanical output, competitive outcome, intervention, retention/transfer)
levels: 1 — some distinction, intervention gap not named
2 — all relevant categories distinguished and the intervention gap named

rubric.criterion: Mechanism stated precisely (impulse, angular momentum, energy flow) rather than as a metaphor
levels: 2 — precise mechanical statement with what must be computed
2 — two or more, including confounding and transfer

rubric.criterion: Loading considered without equating load with injury probability

questions.prompt: Why can't the very high humeral internal-rotation velocity near ball release be explained by the shoulder's internal rotators shortening at that speed alone?

options.text: Because muscles can only lengthen during throwing.
Because of the force–velocity relationship: muscle force and power fall steeply at high shortening velocities, so elastic recoil and segment interaction must contribute.
Because internal rotation is a passive motion with no muscle involvement.
Because the force–length relationship prevents muscles from working at long lengths.

questions.explanation: A muscle shortening near its maximal velocity produces little force and little power. The extreme rotational speeds of throwing therefore depend substantially on elastic energy returned by stretched tissues and on velocity-dependent interaction torques from proximal segments.

optionFeedback.a: Muscles both lengthen and shorten in throwing; the internal rotators lengthen in cocking and shorten in acceleration.
optionFeedback.c: Large net internal-rotation moments act during acceleration; the motion is not passive.
optionFeedback.d: Force–length affects force at extreme lengths but is not the main reason high velocities need other mechanisms.

reserve.prompt: A net shoulder internal-rotation moment of 50 N·m acts while the humerus is externally rotating (moving opposite to the moment) at 30 rad/s. What is the joint power at that instant, in watts? Use a negative sign for absorption.
reserve.working: P = M·ω. The moment and angular velocity have opposite signs, so P = 50 × (−30) = −1,500 W: the moment absorbs energy.
reserve.explanation: Joint power is the product of moment and angular velocity. When the moment opposes the motion, as the internal-rotation moment does during arm cocking, power is negative and energy is absorbed.

reserve.prompt: The ISB recommends a Y–X–Y Euler sequence for the humerus relative to the thorax. At which arm position does this sequence become singular?

options.text: At 90° of elevation.
With the arm hanging at the side (0° elevation) or at 180° elevation.
At 90° of axial rotation.
It has no singular positions.

reserve.explanation: A proper Euler sequence is singular when its middle rotation is 0° or 180°, because the first and third axes then coincide. For Y–X–Y the middle rotation is elevation, so the arm at the side is singular.

optionFeedback.a: Cardan sequences lock at a middle angle of ±90°; Euler sequences do not.
optionFeedback.c: The third rotation does not produce the singularity.
optionFeedback.d: Every three-angle sequence has singular positions.

reserve.prompt: Which of these are best described as task-specific adaptations rather than coordination strategies? Select all that apply.

options.text: Greater humeral retroversion on the throwing side of a professional pitcher
A pitcher's choice of a shorter stride when pitching from the stretch
A shift of the rotational arc toward external rotation in the throwing shoulder
A hitter's decision to widen his stance with two strikes
Hand position adjustments a hitter makes for an inside pitch

reserve.explanation: Retroversion and the accompanying shift of the rotational arc are structural changes associated with years of throwing. Stride length from the stretch, stance width with two strikes and hand adjustments are coordination strategies the athlete chooses or adapts.

stimulus.text: Hypothetical data. Over 40 fastballs, a pitcher's trunk tilt at release varies by ±5° and his shoulder abduction relative to the trunk by ±5°, but release height varies by only ±2 cm. When trunk tilt is larger, shoulder abduction tends to be smaller.

options.text: He is mechanically inconsistent and needs drills to reduce trunk-tilt variability.
Trunk tilt and shoulder abduction co-vary to stabilize release height, consistent with task-relevant control.
The motion-capture system is malfunctioning.
Release height is irrelevant to pitching.

reserve.explanation: Negative co-variation between two joint variables that would otherwise move release height indicates compensation that stabilizes the task variable. That is the pattern predicted by redundancy and optimal feedback control, not inconsistency.

optionFeedback.a: The variability is compensated; reducing it is not justified by these data.
optionFeedback.c: Measurement error would not produce systematic negative co-variation.
optionFeedback.d: Release height affects pitch trajectory and command.

assignment.title: Interpreting a Biomechanics Report

brief.text: You receive the synthetic biomechanics report below for a fictional right-handed pitcher, labelled P-17, captured in two sessions eight weeks apart. Session 1 used the organization's marker-based laboratory; Session 2 used a different vendor's markerless system at a spring facility. A coach has written on the report: “Layback up 12°, abduction at foot contact down, elbow torque up — he's changed his arm action and he's at risk.” Write an interpretation memo for the coach and the director of pitching.

brief.text: Your memo should explain which differences could be definitional or methodological rather than changes in the pitcher, what the kinetics can and cannot say, what can and cannot be concluded about risk, and what you would do next. Use the seven-question standard where it applies, and keep clinical judgements within clinical boundaries.

assignment.deliverable: A 900–1,400-word interpretation memo with a short table classifying each reported difference as likely definitional, possibly methodological, plausibly real, or undeterminable, and a next-step plan.

template.guidance: Three to five sentences: what can be concluded, what cannot, and the recommended next step.

template.guidance: Explain why maximal external rotation and abduction at foot contact are not comparable across the two sessions; refer to reference segments, rotation sequences and the effect of trunk tilt on the arm's position in space.

prompts: Recall a mechanical 'fault' you have corrected or seen corrected. With this week's distinction in mind, was it a physical limitation, a coordination strategy or an adaptation — and what evidence did you have at the time?
Which number in a biomechanics report have you trusted most without asking how it was defined? Write down the three definition questions you would now ask about it.
Think of a kinetic-chain idea you use in your own coaching or evaluation. Which of the five evidence categories actually supports it, and which have you assumed?
Identify one athlete whose movement looks unusual but who performs well. Using Newell's constraints, write two competing explanations for his solution and one measurement that would distinguish them.

review.front: What three things must you know before comparing two 3D shoulder angles?
review.back: The reference segment (for example humerus relative to thorax), the segment axis definitions, and the rotation sequence. Without matching all three, differences may be purely definitional.

review.front: Where do Cardan and proper Euler sequences become singular?
review.back: Cardan (three different axes): when the middle rotation is ±90°. Proper Euler (first and third axes the same): when the middle rotation is 0° or 180°.

review.front: How does contralateral trunk tilt change the arm's position in the laboratory?
review.back: It adds to shoulder abduction in the frontal plane: a 90° abduction with a 30° tilt toward the glove side puts the arm 30° above horizontal.

review.front: What determines the change in an athlete's linear momentum?
review.back: Net impulse — the area under the net force–time curve — not peak force. Vertical impulse must be net of body weight.

review.front: How do you compute a moment from a force?
review.back: M = r × F; magnitude is force times moment arm; direction follows the right-hand rule. Reversing the order flips the sign.

review.front: What is angular impulse equal to?
review.back: The change in angular momentum; for a segment, average moment × time = I × Δω.

review.front: What is a net joint moment, and what is it not?
review.back: The resultant moment at a joint from inverse dynamics, summed over all muscles, ligaments and contact forces. It is not the load on one structure and not an injury probability.

review.front: What does negative joint power mean?
review.back: The net moment opposes the joint's rotation, so the moment absorbs mechanical energy (for example, the internal-rotation moment during arm cocking).
A moment on a segment produced by the motion of linked segments, especially velocity-dependent terms, so proximal rotation can accelerate distal joints without muscle torque there.

review.front: Why do the fastest throwing motions need more than muscle shortening?
review.back: Force–velocity: muscle force and power fall steeply at high shortening velocities, so elastic recoil and segment interaction must contribute.

review.front: What does greater humeral retroversion do to a thrower's shoulder range?
review.back: It shifts the rotational arc toward external rotation, reducing internal rotation while the total arc can stay similar.

review.front: Name the three explanations to consider for a movement difference.
review.back: Physical limitation, motor-control strategy, or task-specific adaptation — each implies a different decision.

review.front: What does energy flow analysis compute?
review.back: Power moving between segments through joint forces and segment torques, from inverse-dynamics outputs; it gives 'transfer' a precise meaning.

review.front: Why is a between-athlete correlation not an intervention effect?
review.back: It compares different athletes, who differ in size, strength and skill; it says nothing about what happens when one athlete changes the variable.
The set of joint configurations that leave a task variable unchanged; more variance along it than across it indicates the variable is stabilized.

review.front: What are Newell's three constraint families?
review.back: Organismic (the performer), environmental (surroundings) and task (goal, rules, implement).
The body has many more degrees of freedom than a task needs; coordination is mastering that redundancy, so skilled repetitions differ in detail while preserving the outcome.

preview.text: This week showed that every biomechanical number is produced by definitions, models and assumptions. Week 2 turns to the instruments that produce those numbers — marker-based and markerless capture, force plates, IMUs, EMG and ball and bat tracking — and to the statistics that tell you whether a measured change is larger than measurement error and normal within-athlete variability.
